modules.title: Conditionals & Modal Verbs
modules.description: Master first and second conditionals along with modal verbs for expressing ability, permission, obligation, and advice.

lessons.title: First Conditional
lessons.description: Learn to express real and possible future situations using if + present simple, will + infinitive.

body.html:
The first conditional describes situations that are real and possible in the future.

Structure: If + present simple, will + infinitive

  • If it rains, I will take an umbrella.
  • If you study hard, you will pass the exam.
  • If she calls me, I will answer.

The if-clause states the condition (present simple). The main clause states the result (will + infinitive).

You can reverse the order: I will take an umbrella if it rains. (No comma when the main clause comes first.)

Common variations: You can replace will with may, might, or can to express different degrees of certainty.
tips: Never use 'will' in the if-clause: 'If it will rain' is WRONG.
Use a comma after the if-clause when it comes first.
The first conditional is about things you believe are genuinely possible.

body.question: Complete the sentence: If you ___ late, you will miss the bus.
body.explanation: In the first conditional, the if-clause uses the present simple ('are'), not 'will be' or past tense forms.

body.sentence: If she ___ her homework, her teacher will be happy.
body.explanation: The if-clause requires the present simple. 'Finishes' is the third-person singular form of 'finish'.

lessons.title: Second Conditional
lessons.description: Express hypothetical or unlikely situations using if + past simple, would + infinitive.

body.html:
The second conditional describes situations that are hypothetical, unlikely, or imaginary.

Structure: If + past simple, would + infinitive

  • If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.
  • If she spoke French, she would work in Paris.
  • If we had more time, we would visit the museum.

Even though we use the past simple, the meaning is about the present or future, not the past.

Special note: With the verb 'be', formal English uses were for all subjects: If I were you, I would accept the offer.
tips: The past simple in the if-clause does NOT refer to past time — it signals unreality.
'If I were you...' is the standard form, even though 'If I was you' is common in speech.
Use 'could' or 'might' instead of 'would' to soften the certainty of the result.

body.question: Which sentence expresses a hypothetical/unlikely situation?
options: If it rains tomorrow, I will stay home.
If I were a millionaire, I would travel the world.
If you finish early, you can leave.
If he calls, tell him I'm busy.
body.explanation: 'If I were a millionaire, I would travel the world' is the second conditional — it describes an imaginary situation, not a real possibility.

body.translation: If I had a car, I would drive to work.

lessons.title: Modal Verbs: Ability & Permission
lessons.description: Use can, could, and may to express ability and ask for or give permission.

body.html:
Modal verbs modify the meaning of the main verb. They express ability, permission, obligation, and more.

Ability

  • can — present ability: She can speak three languages.
  • could — past ability: He could swim when he was five.
  • be able to — used for tenses where can/could don't work: I will be able to help you tomorrow.

Permission

  • can — informal: Can I use your phone?
  • could — more polite: Could I borrow your pen?
  • may — formal: May I leave early today?
tips: Modal verbs are followed by the base form (infinitive without 'to'): 'She can swim', NOT 'She can to swim'.
'Could' for ability refers to the past. 'Could' for permission refers to the present (polite form).
'May' for permission is more formal than 'can'. In everyday speech, 'can' is more common.

body.question: Choose the most polite way to ask for permission: '___ I sit here?'
body.explanation: 'May' is the most formal and polite way to ask for permission. 'Could' is also polite, and 'Can' is informal.

body.sentence: When I was a child, I ___ ride a bicycle without training wheels.
body.explanation: 'Could' expresses general past ability. 'Was able to' is also correct and is preferred for a specific achievement on one occasion.

lessons.title: Modal Verbs: Obligation & Advice
lessons.description: Use must, have to, and should to express obligation, necessity, and recommendations.

body.html:
These modals express different levels of obligation and advice.

Obligation & Necessity

  • must — strong obligation (often internal/personal): I must finish this report today.
  • have to — external obligation or rules: You have to wear a uniform at this school.
  • mustn't — prohibition: You mustn't park here.
  • don't have to — no obligation (it's optional): You don't have to come if you don't want to.

Advice

  • should — recommendation: You should see a doctor.
  • shouldn't — advising against: You shouldn't eat so much sugar.
tips: CRITICAL: 'mustn't' (prohibition) ≠ 'don't have to' (no obligation). They have completely different meanings.
'Must' and 'have to' are often interchangeable, but 'must' feels more personal/internal, while 'have to' implies an external rule.
'Should' is weaker than 'must' — it's advice, not a command.

body.question: You ___ smoke in the hospital. (It is forbidden.)
body.explanation: 'Mustn't' expresses prohibition — it is forbidden. 'Don't have to' means it's not necessary (optional), which is a completely different meaning.

flashcardDecks.title: Conditionals & Modals — Key Terms
flashcardDecks.description: 25 essential grammar terms and example sentences for conditionals and modal verbs at B1 level.

back.text: A structure for real/possible future situations: If + present simple, will + infinitive.
back.example: If it rains, I will take an umbrella.
back.notes: The if-clause uses present simple, NOT 'will'.

back.text: A structure for hypothetical/unlikely situations: If + past simple, would + infinitive.
back.example: If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.
back.notes: The past simple does not refer to the past — it signals unreality.

back.text: The part of a conditional sentence that states the condition.
back.example: 'If you study hard' is the if-clause in 'If you study hard, you will pass.'
back.notes: Also called the 'conditional clause'.

back.text: The part of a conditional sentence that states the result.
back.example: 'you will pass' is the main clause in 'If you study hard, you will pass.'
back.notes: Also called the 'result clause'.

back.text: Imagined or not real; based on a possible situation rather than a real one.
back.example: The second conditional describes hypothetical situations.
back.notes: Adjective. Key concept for understanding the second conditional.

back.text: Modal verb expressing present ability — being able to do something.
back.example: She can speak three languages.
back.notes: Followed by base form (infinitive without 'to').

back.text: Modal verb expressing past general ability.
back.example: He could swim when he was five.
back.notes: For a specific past achievement, prefer 'was able to'.

back.text: Modal verb used to ask for permission politely (more formal than 'can').
back.example: Could I borrow your pen?
back.notes: Present meaning, not past — context determines whether 'could' is about ability or politeness.

back.text: Modal verb used to ask for or give permission (formal).
back.example: May I leave early today?
back.notes: The most formal way to ask permission. More polite than 'can' or 'could'.

back.text: Alternative to 'can' for expressing ability, used in tenses where 'can' is not possible.
back.example: I will be able to help you tomorrow.
back.notes: Use for future ('will be able to'), present perfect ('have been able to'), etc.

back.text: Modal verb expressing strong obligation, often internal or personal.
back.example: I must finish this report today.
back.notes: Stronger than 'should'. No past form — use 'had to' for past.

back.text: Express obligation or necessity, especially from external rules or requirements.
back.example: You have to wear a uniform at this school.
back.notes: Unlike 'must', it has all tenses: 'had to' (past), 'will have to' (future).

back.text: Expresses prohibition — something is forbidden or not allowed.
back.example: You mustn't park here.
back.notes: DIFFERENT from 'don't have to'. Mustn't = forbidden. Don't have to = not necessary.

back.text: Expresses lack of obligation — it is not necessary, but you can if you want.
back.example: You don't have to come if you don't want to.
back.notes: DIFFERENT from 'mustn't'. Don't have to = optional. Mustn't = forbidden.

back.text: Modal verb used to give advice or make recommendations.
back.example: You should see a doctor about that cough.
back.notes: Weaker than 'must'. It's a suggestion, not a command.

back.text: Used to advise against doing something.
back.example: You shouldn't eat so much sugar.
back.notes: Advice, not prohibition. Compare: 'You mustn't' (forbidden) vs 'You shouldn't' (not recommended).

back.text: Modal verb used in the main clause of first conditional sentences to express a future result.
back.example: If you study, you will pass.
back.notes: Never used in the if-clause of conditionals.

back.text: Modal verb used in the main clause of second conditional sentences to express a hypothetical result.
back.example: If I had more time, I would learn Japanese.
back.notes: Can be replaced by 'could' or 'might' for less certainty.

back.text: Modal verb expressing possibility (less certain than 'may').
back.example: If you ask her, she might agree.
back.notes: Can replace 'will' in first conditional or 'would' in second conditional to express uncertainty.

back.text: The infinitive form of a verb without 'to'. Used after all modal verbs.
back.example: She can swim. (NOT 'She can to swim.')
back.notes: Also called the 'bare infinitive'.

back.text: A situation that must be true for something else to happen.
back.example: In 'If it rains, I'll stay home', the rain is the condition.
back.notes: Conditional sentences always have a condition and a result.

back.text: The part of a conditional sentence that describes what happens if the condition is met.
back.example: 'I will stay home' is the result clause in 'If it rains, I will stay home.'
back.notes: Contains 'will' (1st conditional) or 'would' (2nd conditional).

back.text: Something you are required to do, either by rules or personal duty.
back.example: Wearing a seatbelt is a legal obligation.
back.notes: Expressed by 'must' (internal) or 'have to' (external).

back.text: An order that forbids something; something that is not allowed.
back.example: There is a prohibition on smoking in the building.
back.notes: Expressed by 'mustn't' or 'can't' in English.

back.text: Means 'if not'. Used as an alternative to negative if-clauses.
back.example: Unless you hurry, you will be late. (= If you don't hurry, you will be late.)
back.notes: Do not use 'not' with 'unless' — it already contains a negative meaning.

modules.title: Work & Education
modules.description: Build essential vocabulary for talking about jobs, workplaces, applications, education, and technology in professional settings.

lessons.title: Job Titles & Workplaces
lessons.description: Learn common job titles and words related to workplaces and work environments.

body.html:
At B1 level, you should be able to describe jobs and workplaces clearly.

Common Job Titles

  • manager — a person responsible for a team or department
  • employee — a person who works for a company
  • colleague — a person you work with
  • receptionist — a person who greets visitors and answers calls
  • accountant — a person who manages financial records

Workplaces

  • office — a room or building for business work
  • factory — a building where products are manufactured
  • warehouse — a large building for storing goods
  • headquarters — the main office of a company

Work Activities

  • meeting — a gathering to discuss work matters
  • shift — a set period of work (e.g., night shift)
  • overtime — extra hours worked beyond the normal schedule
tips: 'Colleague' and 'coworker' mean the same thing. 'Colleague' is slightly more formal.
'Headquarters' is often shortened to 'HQ' in everyday language.
'Staff' is an uncountable noun in British English: 'The staff are friendly', NOT 'staffs'.

body.question: Products are manufactured in a ___.
body.explanation: A factory is a building where products are manufactured. A warehouse is for storage, not production.

body.sentence: My ___ and I are working on the same project this month.
body.explanation: A 'colleague' (or 'coworker') is a person you work with.

lessons.title: Job Applications
lessons.description: Learn vocabulary related to applying for jobs: CVs, interviews, and employment terms.

body.html:
Understanding job application vocabulary is essential for professional life.

Application Process

  • CV / résumé — a document listing your education, skills, and work experience
  • cover letter — a letter explaining why you want the job
  • application form — a form you fill in to apply for a position
  • interview — a formal meeting where the employer asks you questions
  • candidate — a person applying for a job

Employment Terms

  • salary — the money you earn regularly (usually monthly or annually)
  • experience — knowledge or skill gained from doing something over time
  • qualifications — certificates, degrees, or skills that make you suitable for a job
  • reference — a person who can recommend you to an employer
  • contract — a legal agreement about your job terms
tips: 'CV' (curriculum vitae) is used in British English. 'Résumé' is more common in American English.
'Salary' is for regular (monthly/annual) pay. 'Wage' is usually for hourly or weekly pay.
A 'reference' is both the person AND the letter they write about you.

body.question: A document that lists your education, skills, and work history is called a ___.
body.explanation: A CV (curriculum vitae) or résumé lists your education, skills, and work experience. A cover letter explains your motivation.

body.translation: I submitted my application and got an interview.

lessons.title: Education
lessons.description: Learn vocabulary for academic settings: degrees, courses, exams, and student life.

body.html:
Whether you are talking about your own studies or someone else's, these words are essential.

Academic Terms

  • degree — an academic qualification from a university (e.g., Bachelor's, Master's)
  • course — a series of lessons or lectures on a subject
  • lecture — a talk given to a group of students at university
  • seminar — a smaller, discussion-based class
  • assignment — a piece of work given to students

Assessment

  • exam / examination — a formal test of knowledge
  • grade — a mark showing how well you did
  • pass — to achieve the minimum required grade
  • fail — to not reach the minimum required grade
  • scholarship — money given to a student to pay for their studies
tips: 'Course' in British English = 'program' in American English (for a full degree program).
You 'take' or 'sit' an exam. You 'pass' or 'fail' an exam. You don't 'make' an exam.
'Tuition' means teaching (British) OR the fees paid for education (American).

body.sentence: She received a ___ to study at Oxford, so she didn't have to pay tuition fees.
body.explanation: A 'scholarship' is money awarded to a student to help pay for their studies, often based on academic achievement.

body.question: A piece of work that a teacher gives students to complete is called a(n) ___.
body.explanation: An 'assignment' is a task or piece of work given to students. A 'lecture' is a talk given by a teacher to a class.

lessons.title: Technology at Work
lessons.description: Learn vocabulary related to technology, communication, and project management in the workplace.

body.html:
Modern workplaces rely heavily on technology. These words will help you discuss work tasks and tools.

Communication Tools

  • email — electronic messages sent over the internet
  • attachment — a file sent along with an email
  • inbox — the place where received emails are stored
  • video call — a call where participants can see each other

Project Management

  • deadline — the latest date by which something must be completed
  • project — a planned piece of work with specific goals
  • task — a specific piece of work to be done
  • feedback — comments about the quality of someone's work

Software & Systems

  • software — programs and applications used on computers
  • database — an organized collection of digital information
  • update — a new version or improvement to software
tips: 'Deadline' literally means 'the line of death' — there is no flexibility implied!
'Software' is uncountable: 'a piece of software', NOT 'a software'.
'Feedback' is also uncountable: 'some feedback', NOT 'feedbacks'.

body.sentence: The ___ for this project is next Friday, so we need to finish by then.
body.explanation: A 'deadline' is the latest time or date by which something must be completed.

body.question: A file sent along with an email is called a(n) ___.
body.explanation: An 'attachment' is a file (document, image, etc.) that is sent together with an email.

flashcardDecks.title: Work & Education Vocabulary
flashcardDecks.description: 25 essential words for talking about jobs, workplaces, applications, education, and workplace technology.

back.text: A person responsible for controlling or organizing a team, department, or company.
back.example: She's the manager of the marketing department.
back.notes: Can also be a verb: 'to manage'.

back.text: A person who is paid to work for a company or organization.
back.example: The company has over 500 employees.
back.notes: Opposite: 'employer' (the person/company that hires).

back.text: A person you work with, especially in a professional setting.
back.example: I'm having lunch with a colleague today.
back.notes: Synonym: 'coworker'. 'Colleague' is slightly more formal.

back.text: A building or group of buildings where products are manufactured.
back.example: He works in a car factory outside the city.
back.notes: Plural: 'factories'.

back.text: The main offices of an organization, where central management operates.
back.example: The company's headquarters are in London.
back.notes: Often shortened to 'HQ'. Always plural in form.

back.text: Extra time worked beyond normal working hours, often paid at a higher rate.
back.example: I worked overtime last week to finish the project.
back.notes: Uncountable noun. 'Do/work overtime', NOT 'make overtime'.

back.text: A document that lists your education, work experience, skills, and qualifications.
back.example: Please send your CV with your application.
back.notes: 'CV' = British English. 'Résumé' = American English.

back.text: A formal meeting in which an employer asks a candidate questions about their suitability for a job.
back.example: I have a job interview on Monday morning.
back.notes: Also a verb: 'to interview someone'.

back.text: A fixed regular payment for work, usually expressed monthly or annually.
back.example: Her annual salary is £35,000.
back.notes: 'Salary' = regular pay (monthly/annually). 'Wage' = hourly/weekly pay.

back.text: Knowledge or skill gained from doing a job or activity over time.
back.example: You need at least two years of experience for this role.
back.notes: Uncountable when meaning general experience. Countable when meaning specific events.

back.text: Official records of education, training, or skills that make you suitable for a job.
back.example: What qualifications do you need to become a nurse?
back.notes: Usually plural. 'Qualified' is the adjective.

back.text: A written legal agreement between an employer and employee about job terms.
back.example: I signed a two-year contract with the company.
back.notes: Stress on first syllable as noun. Stress on second syllable as verb.

back.text: An academic qualification awarded by a university after completing a course of study.
back.example: She has a degree in Computer Science.
back.notes: Types: Bachelor's degree, Master's degree, PhD/Doctorate.

back.text: A series of lessons or lectures on a particular subject.
back.example: I'm taking an online course in digital marketing.
back.notes: British: 'course' can mean a full degree program. American: 'course' = single class.

back.text: A formal test of knowledge or ability in a subject.
back.example: The final exams are in June.
back.notes: You 'take' or 'sit' an exam. You 'pass' or 'fail' an exam.

back.text: A task or piece of work given to someone as part of their studies or job.
back.example: The assignment is due next Wednesday.
back.notes: Common collocations: 'hand in / submit an assignment'.

back.text: An amount of money given to a student to help pay for their education, usually based on merit.
back.example: He won a scholarship to study abroad.
back.notes: Different from a 'loan' — a scholarship does not need to be repaid.

back.text: A formal talk given to a group of students at a university.
back.example: I have a lecture on economics at 10 a.m.
back.notes: 'Lecturer' = the person who gives the lecture.

back.text: The latest time or date by which something must be completed.
back.example: We need to meet the deadline for this project.
back.notes: Collocations: 'meet a deadline', 'miss a deadline', 'extend a deadline'.

back.text: A planned piece of work that has a specific purpose and goals.
back.example: We're starting a new project next month.
back.notes: Noun stress: first syllable. Verb stress: second syllable (to project).

back.text: Programs and applications used on computers and electronic devices.
back.example: We use accounting software to manage our finances.
back.notes: Uncountable: 'a piece of software', NOT 'a software'.

back.text: Information or comments about the quality of someone's work, used for improvement.
back.example: The manager gave me positive feedback on my presentation.
back.notes: Uncountable: 'some feedback', NOT 'feedbacks'.

back.text: A file (document, image, etc.) sent along with an email.
back.example: Please find the report in the attachment.
back.notes: Verb: 'to attach'. 'Please see attached' is a common email phrase.

back.text: A set period of work time, especially for workers who work at different times of day.
back.example: She works the night shift at the hospital.
back.notes: Types: day shift, night shift, morning shift.

back.text: A person who provides a recommendation about you, or the letter/statement they provide.
back.example: Can I use you as a reference for my job application?
back.notes: Also called a 'referee' (the person). Employers often ask for two references.

modules.title: Professional Phrasal Verbs
modules.description: Learn and practice phrasal verbs commonly used in workplaces, meetings, and professional communication.

lessons.title: Carry Out & Set Up
lessons.description: Learn phrasal verbs used for completing tasks and organizing things at work.

body.html:
Phrasal verbs are very common in professional English. Here are some used for work tasks.

  • carry out — to perform or complete a task: We need to carry out a full review of the process.
  • set up — to arrange or establish something: Can you set up a meeting for Friday?
  • take on — to accept or begin to handle a responsibility: She took on more work after the promotion.
  • hand in — to submit or give something to someone in authority: Please hand in your reports by Monday.
  • follow up — to take further action after an initial step: I'll follow up with the client tomorrow.
  • wrap up — to finish or complete something: Let's wrap up this meeting.
tips: 'Carry out' is separable: 'carry out a plan' or 'carry a plan out'.
'Set up' is very versatile: set up a meeting, a business, a system, equipment.
'Follow up' is often used with 'on' or 'with': 'follow up on a complaint', 'follow up with a customer'.

body.question: We need to ___ a full investigation into the problem.
body.explanation: 'Carry out' means to perform or conduct. You 'carry out' an investigation, research, a plan, or a task.

body.sentence: Can you ___ a video call with the Tokyo office for tomorrow morning?
body.explanation: 'Set up' means to arrange or organize something so it is ready to use. It's commonly used for meetings, equipment, and systems.

lessons.title: Deal With & Figure Out
lessons.description: Learn phrasal verbs for solving problems and handling challenges at work.

body.html:
These phrasal verbs are essential when talking about problems and solutions in the workplace.

  • deal with — to handle or manage a situation or problem: She deals with customer complaints every day.
  • figure out — to find the answer or solution through thinking: We need to figure out why sales dropped last month.
  • sort out — to resolve or organize something that is confused or problematic: Can you sort out the issue with the printer?
  • come up with — to think of an idea, plan, or solution: He came up with a brilliant marketing strategy.
  • look into — to investigate or examine: I'll look into the matter and get back to you.
  • run into — to encounter an unexpected problem: We ran into some technical issues during the launch.
tips: 'Deal with' is inseparable: 'deal with a problem', NOT 'deal a problem with'.
'Figure out' is separable: 'figure out the answer' or 'figure the answer out'.
'Run into' can also mean to meet someone by chance: 'I ran into my old boss at the café.'

body.translation: We need to figure out a solution.

body.question: He ___ a great idea for the new advertising campaign.
body.explanation: 'Come up with' means to think of or produce an idea, plan, or solution. 'Look into' means to investigate.

lessons.title: Bring Up & Point Out
lessons.description: Learn phrasal verbs for communication, discussions, and meetings in professional settings.

body.html:
In meetings and professional discussions, these phrasal verbs are used constantly.

  • bring up — to introduce a topic into a conversation: She brought up the budget issue at the meeting.
  • point out — to draw attention to something; to highlight a fact: He pointed out several errors in the report.
  • go over — to review or examine something carefully: Let's go over the agenda before we start.
  • put forward — to suggest or propose an idea: She put forward a plan to reduce costs.
  • turn down — to reject or refuse an offer or proposal: They turned down our proposal.
  • come across — to give a particular impression; to seem: He comes across as very confident in meetings.
  • fill in — to give someone the information they need: Can you fill me in on what happened at the meeting?
tips: 'Bring up' is separable: 'bring up a topic' or 'bring a topic up'.
'Go over' is inseparable and means to review. Don't confuse with 'get over' (to recover from).
'Come across' has two meanings: (1) to seem/appear, (2) to find by chance.

body.sentence: She ___ several important issues during yesterday's meeting.
body.explanation: 'Brought up' (past tense of 'bring up') means to introduce a topic into a discussion.

body.question: The auditor ___ three mistakes in the financial report.
body.explanation: 'Pointed out' means to draw attention to something specific, like errors or facts. 'Brought up' means to introduce a topic, not to highlight specific details.

flashcardDecks.title: Professional Phrasal Verbs
flashcardDecks.description: 20 essential phrasal verbs for the workplace, covering tasks, problem-solving, and communication.

back.text: To perform or complete a task, duty, or plan.
back.example: The team carried out a thorough investigation.
back.notes: Separable. Formal synonym: 'conduct', 'execute'.

back.text: To arrange, organize, or establish something.
back.example: Can you set up the projector before the presentation?
back.notes: Separable. Very versatile: set up a meeting, a business, equipment.

back.text: To accept or begin to handle a task, responsibility, or challenge.
back.example: She took on the role of project manager.
back.notes: Separable. Can also mean 'to hire': 'We're taking on new staff.'

back.text: To submit something to a person in authority.
back.example: Please hand in your reports by the end of the day.
back.notes: Separable. Synonym: 'submit', 'turn in' (American English).

back.text: To take further action or check on progress after an initial step.
back.example: I'll follow up with the supplier about the delivery.
back.notes: Often used with 'on' or 'with'. Noun form: 'a follow-up'.

back.text: To finish or conclude something.
back.example: Let's wrap up this discussion and move to the next item.
back.notes: Separable. Very common at the end of meetings.

back.text: To handle, manage, or take action on a problem or situation.
back.example: She deals with customer complaints every day.
back.notes: Inseparable. Synonym: 'handle', 'address'.

back.text: To understand or solve something by thinking about it.
back.example: I can't figure out why the system keeps crashing.
back.notes: Separable. Synonym: 'work out' (British English).

back.text: To resolve, organize, or fix something that is confused or problematic.
back.example: We need to sort out the scheduling conflict.
back.notes: Separable. More common in British English.

back.text: To think of or produce an idea, plan, or solution.
back.example: She came up with a creative solution to the problem.
back.notes: Inseparable (3-word phrasal verb). Synonym: 'think up', 'devise'.

back.text: To investigate or examine something to learn more about it.
back.example: The HR department is looking into the complaint.
back.notes: Inseparable. Synonym: 'investigate', 'examine'.

back.text: To encounter an unexpected problem or difficulty.
back.example: We ran into some difficulties with the new software.
back.notes: Inseparable. Also means 'to meet someone by chance'.

back.text: To introduce a topic into a conversation or discussion.
back.example: He brought up the issue of overtime pay at the meeting.
back.notes: Separable. Also means 'to raise a child'.

back.text: To draw attention to something; to highlight a fact, error, or detail.
back.example: She pointed out that the figures were incorrect.
back.notes: Separable. Often followed by 'that' + clause.

back.text: To review or examine something carefully.
back.example: Let's go over the contract one more time before signing.
back.notes: Inseparable. Synonym: 'review', 'examine'.

back.text: To suggest or propose an idea, plan, or candidate.
back.example: He put forward a proposal to restructure the department.
back.notes: Separable. Synonym: 'propose', 'suggest'.

back.text: To reject or refuse an offer, proposal, or request.
back.example: They turned down our request for extra funding.
back.notes: Separable. Opposite: 'accept', 'take up'.

back.text: To give a particular impression or to seem a certain way.
back.example: She comes across as very professional in interviews.
back.notes: Inseparable. Also means 'to find something by chance'.

back.text: To give someone the information they have missed; to inform.
back.example: Can you fill me in on what was discussed at the meeting?
back.notes: Separable. Also: 'fill in a form' = complete a form.

back.text: To postpone or delay something to a later time.
back.example: We had to put off the meeting until next week.
back.notes: Separable. Synonym: 'postpone', 'delay'. Can also mean 'to discourage'.
